checkpoints: Each `sendMail` call is a full SMTP session — connect, EHLO, AUTH, DATA — so awaiting it directly inside a request handler couples that request's latency, and its very availability, to the health of the mail relay.

In the register handler, `await this.mailService.sendWelcome(...)` sits between the user being created and the HTTP response, so a slow or unreachable SMTP relay makes an otherwise-successful signup hang or time out even though the account was already persisted.

The correct fix is enqueue-and-respond: the controller persists a job (e.g. `mailQueue.add('welcome', { userId, email, name })`) and returns immediately, while a separate worker/processor performs the actual SMTP send outside the request lifecycle, so request latency collapses to the queue-insert time.

The newsletter's `for...await` loop sends to ~10,000 recipients sequentially on a single non-pooled transporter, meaning the whole job runs for hours and every iteration re-pays SMTP connection/handshake overhead instead of reusing a connection.

Because the loop has no per-recipient tracking, a failure partway through (e.g. at recipient #5000) aborts the remaining recipients entirely and leaves no record of who was already sent, making the operation neither resumable nor auditable.

The bulk path should be restructured into one queued job per recipient (e.g. via `addBulk`), with the worker's concurrency and a rate limiter bounded to the relay's actual sending quota, protecting relay limits and sender reputation instead of hammering the relay unbounded.

Persisting per-recipient job state in the queue (e.g. Redis-backed) means a crash mid-run only loses in-flight jobs rather than the whole batch, and jobs can declare retry attempts with exponential backoff to recover automatically from transient SMTP failures.

Moving sends off the request path makes delivery eventual rather than synchronous, so the design needs a dead-letter path plus monitoring for exhausted-retry jobs, and any UI copy claiming an email was 'sent' must be changed to 'queued' since delivery is no longer guaranteed at response time.
